issues.legal_issue: A statutory scheme defining covered land through unguided selection and irrational classifications, without safeguards for affected owners, violates equality and the former constitutional protection of property.
material_facts: The definition covered land that was genuinely unbuilt, land with unauthorised structures selected by an authority, and land placed in a schedule, including land later added by the government without stated criteria.
The authority could select some lands with unauthorised structures and leave similarly situated lands untouched.
The scheme did not distinguish owners who built unauthorised structures from owners whose land had been occupied or built upon by trespassers.

It treated wholly unbuilt plots as covered while excluding plots with even small lawful structures, and the schedule included varied lands without an evident rational connection to the stated purpose.
The statute prescribed no procedure requiring notice or a hearing before the relevant declarations or eviction decisions.
issues.conclusion: The definition of covered land, in each of its parts, violated Articles 14 and 19(1)(f) of the Constitution as it then stood; the Act was unconstitutional, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 requires classifications to rest on a rational basis and to serve the law’s purpose; arbitrary selection and treating materially different persons alike offend that guarantee. Article 19(1)(f), while it remained part of the Constitution, also constrained laws affecting property. Discretion affecting property cannot be left uncontrolled where the scheme lacks standards and safeguards appropriate to the decision. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for these propositions.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and (unguided_land_selection or irrational_classification or no_hearing_before_adverse_decision)

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law governing occupation of land and eviction from it.
predicates.unguided_land_selection: The law permits authorities to select which similarly situated lands are covered without objective standards controlling that choice.
predicates.irrational_classification: The law treats materially different owners or plots alike, or distinguishes between plots without a rational connection to its purpose.
predicates.no_hearing_before_adverse_decision: The law provides no opportunity for affected people to be heard before an adverse declaration or eviction decision.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a land-occupation scheme and the scheme permits unguided selection, irrational classification, or adverse decisions without a hearing, the scheme is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Later procedural rules providing limited notice and an opportunity to object do not cure a law’s original constitutional defects when they leave its discretion unguided and omit comparable safeguards for other decisions.
material_facts: The notice rules were made several years after the Act was passed.
The rules required notice and consideration of objections before certain land declarations and eviction orders.
The rules did not provide a comparable procedure for decisions granting or refusing permission to occupy land.
The rules did not establish guidelines controlling the authority’s discretion in making declarations or eviction decisions.
issues.conclusion: The later rules did not cure the Act’s unconstitutionality.
issues.legal_principle: Procedural rules cannot cure a constitutional defect where they are introduced only after the law’s enactment and, in any event, provide only limited notice protections without supplying the missing standards governing discretion or safeguards for all relevant decisions. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.challenge_to_law_after_procedural_rules: The proceeding challenges a law after procedural rules have been introduced to address decisions made under it.
predicates.rules_leave_discretion_unguided: The rules do not establish objective standards controlling the decision-maker’s discretion.
predicates.rules_omit_safeguards_for_some_decisions: The rules provide notice or an opportunity to object for some decisions but not for other materially relevant decisions.

issues.definition: If a challenge follows the introduction of procedural rules that leave discretion unguided or omit safeguards for some decisions, the original constitutional defect remains uncured.

issues.legal_issue: The state legislature had competence to enact legislation concerning land and the prevention of unauthorised occupation and eviction.
material_facts: The legislation dealt with land in urban areas, unauthorised occupation, and eviction.
The challenge asserted that the state legislature lacked competence to enact the legislation.
issues.conclusion: The state legislature was competent to enact the Act under Entries 18, 64 and 65 of List II.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the subject matter fell within the state legislature’s competence under Entries 18, 64 and 65 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.legislative_competence_challenge: The proceeding challenges whether a state legislature had authority to enact the law.
predicates.state_land_and_occupation_subject_matter: The law concerns land and the regulation of unauthorised occupation and eviction.

issues.definition: When a competence challenge concerns state legislation on land and unauthorised occupation, the state legislature has competence to enact it.

issues.legal_issue: A law that neither transfers ownership of land to the state nor vests in the state the owner’s right to recover rent or compensation does not violate Article 31(1) as applied in this case.
material_facts: The Act regulated occupation of land and allowed the state to collect penal charges from occupiers.
It did not transfer ownership of covered land to the state or a state-controlled corporation.
It did not vest in the state the owner’s or occupier’s right to recover rent or compensation for use and occupation of the land.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not violate Article 31(1) of the Constitution as it then stood.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that Article 31(1) was not violated because the Act did not transfer ownership of land to the state or vest in the state the owner’s or occupier’s right to recover rent or compensation. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.article_31_1_challenge: The proceeding claims that a law violates the constitutional protection against deprivation of property.
predicates.no_transfer_of_land_ownership: The law does not transfer ownership of the affected land to the state or a state-controlled body.
predicates.no_state_vesting_of_recovery_right: The law does not vest in the state the owner’s or occupier’s right to recover rent or compensation for use of the land.

issues.definition: If a property-deprivation challenge concerns a law that transfers neither land ownership nor the relevant recovery right to the state, there is no violation of the protection considered under Article 31(1).

issues.legal_issue: A law that does not transfer the right to possession of private land to the state or its instrumentalities is not a measure of requisition requiring compensation under Article 31(2), and the absence of presidential assent does not invalidate it on that ground.
material_facts: The Act provided for regulation of occupation and possible eviction from land.
It did not transfer the right to possession of covered land to the state, its agents, or its instrumentalities.
The challenge asserted that the Act amounted to requisition without compensation and was invalid for want of presidential assent.
issues.conclusion: The Act did not amount to requisition, did not violate Article 31(2), and was not invalid for want of presidential assent under Article 31(5).
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) was not attracted because the Act did not transfer the right to possession of private land to the state, its agents, or its instrumentalities. Consequently, the asserted requirement of presidential assent under Article 31(5) did not arise. The judgment relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.article_31_2_or_assent_challenge: The proceeding claims that a law requisitions private property without compensation or is invalid for want of required presidential assent.
predicates.no_transfer_of_possession_to_state: The law does not transfer the right to possess private land to the state, its agents, or its instrumentalities.

issues.definition: If a challenge alleges uncompensated requisition or missing assent but the law does not transfer possession of private land to the state or its instrumentalities, there is no requisition-based or assent-based invalidity.
